newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Headlines - Sept 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Headlines - Sept 18.

text.p: These are leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- MING PAO - More than 760,000 signatures have been collected to protest against Japan's claim to the disputed Diaoyu (or Senkaku) Islands, which would be handed to the Japanese consulate.
-- HONG KONG ECONOMIC JOURNAL -- Japan's government would use loans to put pressure on Beijing in the islands dispute.
-- Chairman of Yaohan International Holdings said he was sorrry about the dispute over the Islands and thought China and Japan should establish a relationship of mutual trust.
-- ORIENTAL DAILY -- Taiwan's provincial council had decided to stop buying Japanese goods and ban Japanese companies from entering bids for public projects.

-- Doctors said the artist who gave the statue of Queen Victoria a "facelift" and then showered himself with a can of red paint, might suffer from serious after-effects. A can of paint cost only a few dozen dollars, but it would take $40,000 of taxpayers' money to clean and repair the statue.
-- WEN WEI PO -- Chinese Premier Li Peng listed 10 tasks for the next half of the year, among which was to prepare for the Hong Kong handover.
-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- The disputed Diaoyu Islands would be on the agenda when Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen met his Japanese counterpart in New York next week.

-- The Government was asking for a land premium of $6.4 billion to $6.5 billion -- the highest lump-sum amount charged for a single site -- before a massive $10 billion residential development in Tseung Kwan O could get off the ground.
-- Jardine Matheson Holdings' role in the development of Hong Kong's controversial CT8 and CT9 container terminals had been reduced significantly to gain China's approval.
-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- The Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation came under fire for appointing consultancy chiefs to the top jobs in the West Rail Division.
-- Regional airlines were mulling fare increases if jet fuel prices failed to drop in the coming months.
